title: Don't Touch the Dirt: 6 weeks, ~700 prompts, a browser game built with Claude Code [trailer]
author: Robotron1980
selftext:
Eight college friends, a van stuck in a sinkhole, and something under the desert. Get everyone to the general store before dark. Single player or peer-to-peer co-op, running in the browser on WebGPU.

**Numbers**

- 6 weeks (Sep 28 – Nov 9), about 33 days of actual work
- ~700 prompts over 100 Claude Code sessions. That includes short "yes, do it" replies; substantive requests are maybe two thirds of it
- 221 commits, ~75k lines of TypeScript (sim, client, tests)
- Almost all of it on Claude Opus, with Sonnet for some subagents

**Tools**

- **Claude Code** (desktop app): code, Blender models, audio processing, the trailer score. It also ran and playtested the game in its built-in browser: ~5,000 JavaScript probes into the running page and ~1,000 clicks and screenshots, checking its own changes
- **three.js** (WebGPU renderer, TSL shaders), **Rapier** physics, **Vite**, **TypeScript**, **Vitest**
- **PeerJS** for co-op: the host's browser runs the simulation, with no game server
- **Blender**, driven by Claude through an MCP bridge: every vehicle and building is a Python build script (box modeling and lofts, not primitive kitbash), modeled from reference photos and blueprints
- **Mixamo** for character bases and animation clips
- **ChatGPT / Codex image generation**: key art and store capsules, plus painting textures over Claude's clay renders of the models (~50 image prompts)
- **Sound**: CC0 field recordings (BigSoundBank, freesound), cut and mixed by Python scripts. The trailer score is no AI music generator: Claude synthesized it in Python (numpy) with CC0 orchestral samples (VSCO 2 Community Edition). It can't hear, so it checked levels and spectra by measurement while I listened and gave notes. Several rounds came out too heroic, too whimsical or too "video game" before landing on a slow 1950s B-monster march
- **Trailer edit**: footage captured with **OBS** using a capture mode in the game that hides all UI, cut in **DaVinci Resolve**

**Stages (prompts in each)**

1. **Prototype, days 1–4 (~165).** The worm chase, stealth and a tremor-meter HUD, flares, survival systems, townsfolk, a first co-op server.
2. **World and art, week 2 (~70).** Blender art pass, destructible wooden buildings the worm bursts through, drivable pickup and tractor, an 8×3 km valley streamed around the player, peer-to-peer co-op in place of the server.
3. **Design reset (inside stage 2).** I stopped and wrote a design doc before building more. The mission/stash/save loop was cut, and the game became one run: the van in the sinkhole, the store at dark, play as any of the cast.
4. **Content, weeks 3–4 (~155).** The cast modeled and rigged, being caught and swallowed, tools (shovel, chainsaw, dynamite, rifle), a second creature at sundown, road and utility crews with their machines (bucket truck, bulldozer, semi). Bots play each character's route through the level as automated tests.
5. **Feel and polish, week 4 (~220, the busiest).** Hands on props, followers that walk your trail and climb your rock, real recorded gunshots and chainsaw, shooting balance, an ambushed demo mode.
6. **Trailer and performance, weeks 5–6 (~90).** The score and capture mode; then a locked 30 fps on an Intel iGPU and 60 on a desktop GPU, getting it to load on an iPhone's Safari (GPU memory from 650 MB down to ~220), and a co-op desync hunt.

**What worked**

- Settling the design before the implementation. Most of my wasted prompts came from building before the design was settled.
- Telling it what's wrong in plain words and giving references: film stills, real photos, "this looks like shiny plastic." It keeps notes on my corrections between sessions.
- Bots that play the level as tests, so a tuning change that breaks a route shows up right away.
- Measuring instead of guessing: a frame profiler and load logs it reads itself, and on-device error screens for the phone.

**Play it:** https://playharmony.ai/share/6ed50d48/Dont-Touch-the-Dirt

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
Ahh. I am in a different boat of how active I am in my game design with Claude. 20k replies in a week. 

I asked Claude for this week's (yesterday so it’s last weeks)

This week on this Mac came to about 3.03 billion tokens.

•	⁠Who used it: workflow agents 2.48 billion (82%), our chat sessions 0.55 billion. All of it was Opus 5.5, across 20,523 replies.  
•	⁠Against the limit: that’s what took this account to 93% of its week.
